title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
gist: Ladybird, a browser with an engine and LibJS JavaScript engine written from scratch (not a Blink/Gecko/WebKit fork), released its first downloadable auto-updating alpha for macOS and Linux on November 23 after four years of work. The reviewer found it surprisingly capable on Google Maps, GitHub and YouTube, though it is explicitly not secure enough for daily use; its value is as a fourth independent engine that exposes Chromium-specific web dependencies.

insights.claim: Nearly the entire modern web runs on three browser engines — WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox) and Blink (Chromium) — with Chrome, Edge, Brave and Opera all built on Google's Blink.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Engine monoculture gives Google outsized control over web platform direction.

insights.claim: Because most traffic runs on Chromium, web developers optimize for it and the whole web platform tends to follow whatever the dominant engine supports.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Reinforces Google's de facto standard-setting power, relevant to antitrust scrutiny of Chrome.
insights.locator: Those limited options mean that web developers

insights.claim: An independent browser engine like Ladybird is unlikely to shift market share soon but adds a standards implementation that surfaces Chromium-specific assumptions and pushes the ecosystem toward the spec.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Ladybird's significance is ecosystem/standards leverage, not a near-term competitive threat to incumbents.
insights.quote: every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against
insights.locator: An independent implementation of web standards

insights.claim: Ladybird released its first downloadable alpha on November 23 after four years of from-scratch engine development, offering prebuilt auto-updating rolling releases for macOS and Linux, with Windows support planned.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Moving from compile-from-source to installable packages is the step needed for user adoption.
insights.quote: The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,
insights.locator: After four years of work to build a browser engine

insights.claim: The Ladybird Browser Initiative is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations, with no sponsored search engine deals and no sponsor say over the roadmap; its default search engine is None.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Contrasts with browsers dependent on search-default payments — a model insulated from search-deal remedies.

insights.claim: Ladybird began in C++ out of SerenityOS but has started shifting toward Rust, beginning with its JavaScript engine.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Another sign of Rust adoption for memory-safety in security-critical software.
insights.locator: Though the browser began as C++

insights.claim: Ladybird lead Andreas Kling warns the alpha makes no security promises and invites security researchers to hack it.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Not enterprise-ready; adoption limited to enthusiasts for now.
insights.quote: We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.
insights.locator: While it’s exciting to have a new engine option

insights.claim: In testing on a Ryzen 7 mini PC under Fedora Linux, Ladybird alpha 2026.47.8 handled tabbed browsing, Google Maps including Street View, GitHub and YouTube smoothly, stalling only after repeated seeking in a 4K stream with about 10 tabs open.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: A small donation-funded team reaching usable compatibility suggests browser engine barriers to entry are lower than assumed.
insights.quote: the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software

insights.claim: The reviewer concludes a small donation-funded team has built a from-scratch browser engine that handles real web browsing, though it won't replace Firefox for him soon and is not yet trustworthy as a daily driver.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Watch Ladybird's beta/Windows timeline as a gauge of a credible non-Chromium alternative.
